The entry form for the state painting competition had to be uploaded by 5 p.m., and the only working computer in the school library was painfully slow. Dolma had her painting of the monastery festival photographed on her phone.
Anirban, beside her, had already uploaded his. "Go on, it's 4:30," he said.
Dolma held the phone and didn't move. If she entered and came nowhere, everyone would know. If she didn't enter, at least nobody could say she'd lost.
"The upload's too slow anyway," she said.
At 5:01 the portal closed. That night she looked at the painting for a long time and felt a quieter, heavier kind of disappointment.

qa.q: What was Dolma's painting of?
qa.a: Her painting was of the monastery festival.

qa.q: Why did not entering feel safer to Dolma at 4:30?
qa.a: She feared the regret and embarrassment of entering and coming nowhere more than the loss of never trying, so doing nothing felt protective.

qa.q: At what moment could Dolma have chosen differently, and what could she tell herself?
qa.a: When Anirban said 'Go on', she could have uploaded and reminded herself that not entering is also a result she might regret.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel when the portal closes without Dolma's entry?
qa.a: Anirban may feel sorry for her and a bit frustrated, having urged her on while the chance slipped away.

grounding: Shows a teenager who avoids entering a competition because failing feels worse than not trying, then feels a quieter regret.

In the lift of their Bengaluru apartment block, Uday stood next to Pallavi from the eighth floor, rehearsing in his head: "Want to go to the book fair on Saturday?" He'd practised it all week.
Floor three. Floor four. If she said no, he'd have to see her in this lift every day and remember it. If he never asked, nothing could go wrong.
Floor seven. Pallavi smiled, said, "Bye, Uday," and stepped out at eight.
Uday rode up to the twelfth floor alone, the sentence still in his mouth. That evening he saw her photo from the book fair with friends on the building group and wondered what she would have said.

qa.q: Where did Uday want to invite Pallavi?
qa.a: To the book fair on Saturday.

qa.q: Why did staying silent feel safer to Uday in the lift?
qa.a: He imagined the sting of a no every day in the same lift, so not asking felt like it protected him from any regret.

qa.q: What small step could help Uday next time he wants to ask?
qa.a: He could ask early in the ride instead of waiting for the right floor, and remind himself that not asking also leaves a 'what if'.

qa.q: How might things look from Pallavi's side?
qa.a: Pallavi only sees a quiet neighbour in the lift; she never knew about the invitation, so she had no chance to say yes or no.

grounding: Shows a teenager who never asks a neighbour to an outing because a refusal feels worse than never trying.

"The debate trials are tomorrow, Ira. Did you sign up?" Pema asked, stirring the thukpa.
"No, Ama."
"You practise speeches in the bathroom every morning."
"That's the bathroom. If I go to trials and get cut, the whole class will see."
"And if you don't go?"
"Then nobody sees anything. Nothing happens."
Pema turned off the stove. "Nothing happening is also something. Remember last year's science fair? You didn't enter, and you kept saying yours was better than the winner's."
Ira pulled at a thread on her sleeve. "That was different."
"Was it?"
Ira was quiet. Then: "Sign-up closes at eight?"
"Seven-thirty. You have twenty minutes."

qa.q: What was Pema cooking?
qa.a: Pema was stirring the thukpa.

qa.q: Why did not signing up feel sensible to Ira?
qa.a: Ira feared the whole class seeing her get cut, and thought that if she stayed away, nothing bad could happen.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation?
qa.a: Pema's reminder of the science fair Ira skipped, which showed that not trying had already left her with regret.

qa.q: How does Pema see her daughter's fear?
qa.a: Pema knows Ira practises every morning and wants her to see that sitting out is also a choice that costs something.

grounding: Shows a teenager who avoids trying out for fear of failing publicly, until her mother points to an earlier regret of not trying.

passage: Last month the district science fair opened entries, and my friend Santosh kept saying, "Your bottle water filter is perfect for it, Lalit." I carried the form in my bag for two weeks. Every night I pictured the judges walking past my table to the city school kid with the robot, and the results sheet on the notice board without my name. Then I'd picture Papa asking, "So, how did it go?" That picture felt worse than anything. So I told myself the fair was for kids with labs at home, and I let the deadline pass. Santosh took his solar cooker and came fourth. Fourth isn't a prize, but he got to talk to a real scientist for ten minutes. Now I think about that more than I ever thought about losing.

qa.q: How long did Lalit carry the science fair form in the bag?
qa.a: For two weeks.

qa.q: Why did letting the deadline pass feel safer to Lalit at the time?
qa.a: Lalit kept picturing losing, a missing name on the results sheet and Papa's question, and that imagined regret felt worse than not trying at all.

qa.q: Where was the turning point Lalit let slip, and what could Lalit do differently next time?
qa.a: The two weeks with the form in the bag were the chance; next time Lalit could fill it in on the first day, before the imagined failure grows.

qa.q: How might Santosh see Lalit's choice not to enter?
qa.a: Santosh believed the filter was perfect for the fair, so he may feel disappointed and wonder why his friend didn't trust the idea.

grounding: A teenager looks back on skipping a science fair because the imagined regret of failing felt worse than never trying.

passage:
Coach's note, Sunday. Tanvir, junior swim squad.
Damini (15) swam the fastest 100m freestyle in practice this month. When I handed out forms for the state trials, she took one, folded it and left it on the bench. Asked why, she said, "If I go and don't make it, everyone will know I thought I was good enough." It's easier, she added, to say she just didn't feel like it. She laughed while saying this but kept picking at her swim cap.
What I did next: I didn't push. I showed her last year's qualifying list, where several times were slower than hers, and asked her to imagine next year's trials having never tried this one. She went quiet. On Monday she brought the form back, half filled. I've told her we'll prepare together and look at the result together, whatever it is.

qa.q: What did Damini do with the trials form at first?
qa.a: She took one, folded it and left it on the bench.

qa.q: What does Damini picking at her swim cap while laughing suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the laugh covered real worry; she feared the regret and embarrassment of not qualifying more than the quiet loss of skipping 😰

qa.q: What was the turning point in Coach Tanvir's approach, and why did it work?
qa.a: Instead of pushing, the coach asked Damini to picture next year having never tried, which made the regret of not trying feel real too.

qa.q: What would it mean for Coach Tanvir if Damini had not brought the form back?
qa.a: The coach would likely feel sad to see a strong swimmer miss a chance, and might wonder what else could have helped.

grounding: A coach records a teenager who would rather skip state trials than risk the regret of failing, and how picturing the regret of not trying shifts her.

passage: The district kabaddi trials were in Satara on Sunday, and the bus left Wai at six in the morning. Yogesh had practised all summer on the dusty ground behind the temple. On Saturday night, lying awake, he pictured it: the big boys from the city clubs, the coach's clipboard, his name not on the list, the whole village knowing by evening. It seemed safer not to go at all. Then nobody could say he had failed. At six he heard the bus horn and pulled the sheet over his head. Vikas went alone. He didn't get selected either, but the coach told him to come back next year and gave him a training schedule. When Vikas showed him the schedule, Yogesh felt something worse than failing would ever have been.

qa.q: Where were the district kabaddi trials?
qa.a: The trials were in Satara.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh pull the sheet over his head instead of catching the bus?
qa.a: Yogesh felt afraid of not being selected and of the whole village knowing, so not trying seemed safer than a visible failure.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do to be ready for next year's trials?
qa.a: Ask Vikas to share the training schedule, practise with him, and remember that trying and missing still leads somewhere.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel after going alone and not being selected?
qa.a: Vikas might feel disappointed but encouraged, with a coach's invitation and a schedule to work towards.

grounding: Shows a teenager skipping a sports trial to avoid the regret of failing, then feeling the sharper regret of not trying.

passage: All week in Prague, Jana practised the sentence: "Do you want to go to the spring dance with me?" She said it to the mirror, to her cat, to the tram window. Daniel sat two rows ahead in maths, drew rockets on his hands, and laughed at her jokes. But every time she got close, a picture flashed up: him saying no, kindly, and her walking back to her seat while the whole row watched. Better not to ask, she decided. Then nothing could go wrong. On Friday she heard Daniel tell a friend he was going with his cousin's group, because "nobody asked me anyway." Jana looked down at her desk. Nobody asked. She had asked a hundred times, to the mirror.

qa.q: What did Daniel draw on his hands?
qa.a: Daniel drew rockets on his hands.

qa.q: Why did Jana decide not to ask Daniel?
qa.a: Jana felt scared of a kind no and of the whole row watching, so the regret of being turned down seemed worse than never asking.

qa.q: What could Jana try the next time she wants to ask someone something like this?
qa.a: Picture both regrets side by side, including never knowing, and ask privately, away from the whole row, so a no would feel smaller.

qa.q: What would change if Jana had asked?
qa.a: Daniel, who said nobody asked, might well have said yes, or at least Jana would know instead of wondering.

grounding: Shows a teenager avoiding asking someone to a dance, fearing the regret of a no more than the regret of never asking.

The notice on the school board said: Inter-school Science Fair, entries close Friday. Neelam read it three times during lunch.

"Your water filter idea would win something," said Simran, holding out the form.

"Or it'd fall apart in front of judges from six schools."

"So?"

Neelam folded the form into a tiny square. "If I don't enter, nobody can say it was bad."

In chemistry lab, she kept glancing at her old sketch in the back of her notebook. On Thursday evening she almost filled the form, then put it back in her bag.

On Saturday Simran messaged her a photo of the prize table. Neelam looked at it for a long time and didn't reply.

qa.a: It said Inter-school Science Fair, entries close Friday.

Dear Elizabeth,

You asked if I'd told Harleen how I feel. I didn't. I had it all planned for the school trip on Saturday. I'd even practised what to say. Then on the bus I kept picturing her face going blank and everyone finding out. I thought, if she says no, I'll regret it forever. So I talked about the museum instead.

Now it's Tuesday and she's been sitting with someone else at lunch. I keep telling myself that at least I didn't get rejected. But it doesn't feel like a win. It feels like I left a question open that will never close.

Next time, I think I'd rather hear no than hear nothing.

Write back soon,
Gurpreet

qa.a: Gurpreet planned to talk to Harleen on the school trip on Saturday.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet afraid of on the bus?
qa.a: Gurpreet was scared of Harleen saying no and feared the lasting regret and embarrassment of rejection.

qa.q: What could Gurpreet try when a similar chance comes up again?
qa.a: Gurpreet could say the simple words early, before the what-ifs grow, and accept that a clear no is easier to live with than never knowing.

qa.a: Elizabeth might feel sympathy for Gurpreet and want to encourage trying next time, since the regret of not asking is clear in the letter.

Can I tell you something embarrassing? I'm Aadhya, and in class ten there was this state-level debate competition. My English teacher said I should apply. My best friend Preeti even printed the form for me.

I kept it in my maths book for two weeks. Every time I thought about it, I pictured myself forgetting my points on stage. Then I'd feel better if I just... didn't. I told myself not trying was the smart option. No failure, no regret.

The deadline passed. Preeti went instead, and she came third. I clapped for her, I really did. But on the bus home I was quiet. I kept thinking, that could have been my third place, or even my last place, and at least I'd know.

qa.q: Where did Aadhya keep the debate form for two weeks?
qa.a: Aadhya kept the form in a maths book for two weeks.

qa.q: Why did not applying feel like "the smart option" to Aadhya?
qa.a: Picturing forgetting points on stage made Aadhya anxious, and skipping felt like relief from the risk of failure and regret.

qa.q: What would you advise Aadhya to do with the next competition form?
qa.a: Submit it soon, maybe with Preeti's help, and remember that even a last place teaches more than never knowing.

qa.q: What might Preeti have felt coming third while her friend stayed home?
qa.a: Preeti may have felt proud of her result but also a little sad that Aadhya wasn't there with her.

grounding: A teenager avoids applying for a competition, fearing the regret of failing more than never trying, and later feels the regret of inaction.

Monday. The notice went up: auditions for the inter-school singing competition on Friday. Uday stood in front of it for a long time. Madhuri, beside him, said, "You have to go. You sing on the bus every day."
"What if I get rejected in front of everyone?" he said. "I'll feel stupid for weeks. If I don't go, nothing bad happens."
Friday. From the corridor, Uday heard the auditions through the music room door. One boy sang off-key and still laughed. Madhuri went in, sang, and came out grinning. Uday walked away before his name was called.
Two weeks later. The school team sang at the district finals, and Uday watched from the audience. They came third. On the way home he couldn't stop thinking: what if I'd been up there? It felt worse than any rejection he had imagined.

qa.q: When were the auditions?
qa.a: The auditions were on Friday.

qa.q: Why did Uday walk away before his name was called?
qa.a: Uday was afraid of being rejected in front of everyone and feeling stupid for weeks, which felt worse than not trying.

qa.q: What could Uday tell himself before the next audition?
qa.a: Uday could remember how bad the 'what if' felt after the finals, and that trying and failing is often easier to live with than never trying.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel watching Uday walk away?
qa.a: Madhuri might feel disappointed and a bit sad, having encouraged Uday because he sings on the bus every day.

grounding: Shows a teenager who avoids an audition because the regret of failing feels worse than never trying, until the regret of not trying arrives.

Uma, you're not entering the science fair because you might not win? Sit down. I'm your Kishore Mama, and I want to tell you about a form I never posted.
When I was sixteen, our coach gave me a form for the state under-seventeen cricket trials. I was good, you know. Really good. But I kept thinking: if I go and they send me home in the first round, the whole town will know. I'll have to live with that. If I don't go, I can always say I might have made it.
I kept the form in my school bag for three weeks and never posted it.
A boy from the next village went. He didn't get selected either. But he came back and played club cricket for twenty years, and he never once wondered.
I still wonder. Fifty years later, I still wonder.

qa.q: How long did Kishore keep the form in the school bag?
qa.a: Kishore kept the form in the school bag for three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Kishore never post the form?
qa.a: Kishore was afraid of being sent home in the first round and the whole town knowing, so avoiding that regret felt safer.

qa.q: Which choice in the story could have changed things for Kishore, and why?
qa.a: Posting the form, because even losing, like the boy from the next village, would have ended fifty years of wondering.

qa.q: How might the boy from the next village have felt after not being selected?
qa.a: He likely felt disappointed for a while but free of 'what if', going on to play club cricket for twenty years.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a teenage choice not to try out for fear of failing, and the longer regret of never trying.

The online entry for the national young poets' competition closed at 5 p.m., and at 4:05 Bhavna was in the cyber cafe near the bus stand with her poem on a pen drive and a crowd of boys shouting over a game behind her.
She had opened the form three times that week and closed it three times. If she lost, she'd know for sure she wasn't good. If she didn't send it, she could still believe she might be.
"Just upload it," Shalini said, leaning over her shoulder.
"What if it's bad?"
"Then you'll know, and you'll write a better one. What if it's good and you never sent it?"
At 4:47 the cafe's internet dropped. Bhavna felt, to her surprise, a flash of panic. She wanted it sent.
At 4:56 the line came back. She clicked submit, hands shaking, while the boys behind her cheered at their game.

qa.a: The online entry closed at 5 p.m.

qa.q: Why had Bhavna closed the form three times that week?
qa.a: Bhavna was afraid of losing and knowing for sure she wasn't good, so not sending it felt safer than the regret of failing.

qa.q: Which question from Shalini helped, and why?
qa.a: 'What if it's good and you never sent it?', because it made the regret of not trying feel real too.

Paper stars hung in the corridor of Aadhya's Chandigarh school for Christmas week when the notice for the inter-school poetry slam went up. Entries closed Friday.
"You have to," Jasleen said, tapping the poster. "Your monsoon poem made Ma'am cry."
Aadhya pictured it: the auditorium, her voice cracking on the second verse, the judges' blank faces, kids from other schools whispering. Worse, she pictured the ride home knowing she'd been bad. "If I don't enter, at least I can't lose," she said.
On Thursday Jasleen slid a form onto her desk, already half filled. Aadhya held the pen over it for a long moment, then tucked it into her notebook.
On Saturday Jasleen texted the list of finalists. Aadhya read every name and felt a small, sour ache she hadn't expected.

qa.q: When did entries for the poetry slam close?
qa.a: Entries closed Friday.

qa.q: Why does not entering feel safer to Aadhya?
qa.a: She is afraid of failing on stage and of the ride home knowing she'd been bad, so not trying feels like a way to avoid that regret.

qa.q: What could Aadhya try the next time a chance like this comes?
qa.a: She could picture both regrets side by side, a shaky voice on stage and reading the finalists' list from home, and ask herself which she would rather live with.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel when the form stays in Aadhya's notebook?
qa.a: Jasleen may feel disappointed, since she believed in the monsoon poem enough to half fill the form herself.
